newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Chechnya, seek Caspian oil transit solution.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Chechnya, seek Caspian oil transit solution.

text.p: Moscow and Chechnya are working furiously to smooth out major uncertainties over what role the independence-minded Russian republic will play in transporting some of the world's newest oil to Western markets.
Industry executives and officials said on Tuesday negotiations with Chechnya were a volatile cocktail of geopolitics and economics but that a solution was in sight.

"As you can see, the situation is very hard," said Emir Gantemirov, chief Moscow representative of Chechnya's Southern Oil Company, known as YUNKO. "But I hope the situation will be resolved because Chechnya needs money. I am optimistic."

In the drama's latest chapter, Azeri President Haydar Aliyev and the head of Azeri state oil company SOCAR, Natik Aliyev, are due to arrive in Moscow mid-week to discuss oil and other issues with top Russian officials.

Interfax news agency quoted Chechen First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov as saying his delegation had signed banking and customs agreements on Tuesday and that the deals could facilitate a long-delayed oil transport agreement.

Azerbaijan, host to an $8 billion, 13-member international oil group due to start producing in the Azeri sector of the Caspian Sea in August, wants to make sure its first oil will go through Russia, including through Chechnya, as planned.

The consortium, the British Petroleum -Statoil -led Azerbaijan International Operating Company, or AIOC, said it would not interfere in the negotiations, which it called a governmental, not corporate, issue.
"AIOC is optimistic negotiations are proceeding well," said AIOC spokeswoman Tamam Bayatly in Baku. "But this is an internal affair between Russia and Chechnya. AIOC is not involved."

The southern separatist region of Chechnya, which fought a bloody, 21-month war with Moscow in a failed secession bid, is playing its card by demanding a share in profits from the transport of AIOC oil via a Russian pipeline across Chechnya.
The war left tens of thousands dead before Russian troops withdrew in humiliation last August, leaving Chechnya and its small oil industry in ruins but the pipeline largely intact.
About 160 km of the nearly 1,500 km pipeline linking Baku and Russia's Black Sea oil export outlet of Novorossiisk run through Chechnya, including via the war-ravaged capital Grozny.

All parties involved have been wrangling for months over the transport deal, needed soon since AIOC will start producing at its Caspian Chirag field on August 28. Chechnya wants big transit revenues and a greater managing role, while Moscow says this is inappropriate since Chechnya is part of Russia.
It will take four months for AIOC oil to fill the pipeline at the Azeri-Russian border, making the end of December the earliest new Caspian oil would cross Russia to world markets.
Transneft says $2 million and only 20 days are needed to refurbish and commission the Chechen link. But other forces are at play.

"The issue requires a lot of coordination on various levels and there are a lot of political questions," said Ravil Polyanin, spokesman for Transneft, the Russian oil pipeline monopoly which has a deal with AIOC to transport the oil.

Transneft wants its own agreement with YUNKO, since the monopoly is obliged under agreements with AIOC to make sure the oil flows through its pipelines, but is worried that Grozny's discord with Moscow could spoil things.

Under its agreement with Transneft, AIOC will pay $15.67 per tonne of oil in transit fees to send its crude through the link. Gantemirov said Transneft had proposed Chechnya get $1.65 per tonne but said it was below the $2.09 YUNKO wanted.
YUNKO also wants Russia, AIOC and Transneft to set up what Gantemirov called a coordinating firm to deal with operational issues like transport and oil supplies to Chechen refineries.

AIOC, which will also use a Western route to Georgia's Supsa port for its so-called early output, still needs the Russian link, since the western link requires extensive refurbishing and construction and will not be ready until end-1998.

The issue of where to build a brand new pipeline to carry AIOC's main output, to peak at 700,000-800,000 barrels per day by 2007-2010, is another hornet's nest of geopolitics, with Georgia, Russia, Armenia among the possible routes. But AIOC said that at least the early oil would go as planned.
"We won't need the Russian pipeline system until the end of the year," Bayatly said, adding there was time for all to sign transport agreements. "There are no reasons to worry."
